notes: \cpara{Sets up the first koan. The friend's charge rests on two observations: the time the novice spends listening to his master, and his talk of ``rational'' this and that.}
\cpara{The novice asks for reassurance that the teachings are not ``only dogma.''}
\cpara{The master's first answer: a tool's worth shows in use, not in what it would fetch. The long speech below says the same in plain words.}
\cpara{The novice objects to the style of the answer, a joke the post makes at its own expense.}
\cpara{The master promises plain arguments on one condition, a silly hat.}

\cpara{The lesson, stated plainly. The novice obeyed an arbitrary order in order to be reassured, and a worse master could have charged him ``a hundred silver coins.'' The koan thus grants the friend's worry about obedience, and places the cure in the novice's motives: be curious, test the method on real questions, and stop watching to see who is laughing.}

\cpara{The moral in the successor's rule: ``Use the techniques and do not mention them.'' Nine days later ``Cultish Countercultishness'' states the lesson in prose, repeats the image of the swordsman who glances away ``to see if anyone might be laughing,'' and points back to these koans in a footnote.}
\cpara{The second koan. The worry is now about the dojo's practices, not its teachings.}
\cpara{The novice's evidence: robes and hoods, which make the dojo look like the Freemasons.}
\cpara{The master repeats the demand for a silly hat. This time the novice refuses to see how it could help.}

\cpara{The master answers as if the worry were about reasoning: clothing has nothing to do with probability theory, so a hat is as good as a robe. The novice's first complaint was that the dojo is ``a little cultish,'' and ``Every Cause Wants To Be A Cult,'' nine days earlier, traced cultishness to ordinary in-group feeling, not to bad reasoning. Whether shared robes feed that feeling is a question the koan does not take up.}
\cpara{Ends with the novice in a clown suit. The name is presumably a play on Bozo, a well-known clown. The koan leaves the reader to decide whether he learned the lesson or overlearned it.}
